lesson_title: The Car Lot Detective: Growth and Decay
hook_text: A bakkie cost R250 000 new. Three years later: R128 000. One cube root exposes exactly what it loses every year.
clip_script: Walk onto the car lot. This bakkie cost 250 000 rand new, three years ago. Today it's priced at 128 000. Question: what percentage does it shed every single year? Time to be a detective. Reducing-balance decay means the value was multiplied by the same mystery factor, three years running. First move — always — divide end by start: 128 000 over 250 000 is 0,512. Just over half the value survived. Now un-multiply. One year's factor is the number that multiplies by itself three times to give 0,512 — the cube root. And 0,8 times 0,8 is 0,64, times 0,8 again... 0,512. Exactly. Each year the bakkie kept 80 percent. It sheds 20 percent per annum — that's the hidden rate, extracted with one division and one root. Sense check: decay factors must land BELOW one. If your root comes out above one, your fraction went in upside down. Divide, root, read the distance from one. That's how you price any depreciating machine in the country — and the same trick, flipped above one, exposes any secret growth rate too.
visual_style: A dusty car lot, price tags morphing from 250 000 to 128 000, a magnifying glass over a shrinking bakkie, three times-0,8 stamps landing year by year, a factor dial pointing below one.
mood: Detective-cool, satisfying, a case cracked clean.
pacing: Slow reveal of the evidence, quick calculated strikes through the division and root, confident verdict.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and extract the hidden rate from any pair of prices.
